questions.q: The mass defect of a nucleus is best defined as which quantity?
options: The total mass of the separate constituent protons and neutrons of the nucleus
The difference between the mass of a nucleus and the total mass of its constituent nucleons
The mass of a nucleus expressed in atomic mass units rather than kilograms
The mass of an electron that is lost when the nucleus forms
questions.explanation: The mass of any nucleus is not the sum of the masses of its constituent protons and neutrons. The difference between the mass of a nucleus and the total mass of its constituent nucleons is the mass defect, and it is always positive for a bound nucleus.

questions.q: A proton and a neutron combine to form a deuterium nucleus, releasing energy. The mass defect of the deuterium nucleus is 0.002 388 u. Calculate the binding energy of the deuterium nucleus in MeV.
working: The \(c^{-2}\) is already baked into the 931.5 conversion factor, so you do NOT also divide by \(c^2\).
questions.explanation: Using the standard conversion that the energy equivalent of 1 u is 931.5 MeV, the binding energy of a deuterium nucleus is 0.002 388 × 931.5 = 2.224 MeV — the energy released when a proton and neutron combine, or required to separate them again.

questions.q: Using the data-sheet conversion 1 u = 931.5 MeV c⁻², how do you convert a mass defect in atomic mass units into a binding energy in MeV?
options: Multiply the mass defect in u by 931.5, then also divide by the speed of light squared
Multiply the mass defect in u by 931.5; the c⁻² is already part of the conversion factor, so you do not divide by c² as well
Divide the mass defect in u by 931.5 to obtain the energy in MeV
Convert the mass defect to kilograms, which directly gives the binding energy in MeV
questions.explanation: It is much easier to use the conversion that the energy equivalent of 1 u is 931.5 MeV, written on data sheets as 1 u = 931.5 MeV c⁻². The c⁻² is part of the unit, so the c² is already done for you — multiplying by 931.5 and also dividing by c² is the most common error on this calculation.

questions.q: The mass of a helium-4 atom is 4.002 603 u, and the total mass of its constituents (two protons, two neutrons and two electrons) is 4.032 980 u. Calculate the average binding energy per nucleon of helium.
questions.given: total mass of constituents \(= 4.032\,980\,\mathrm{u}\);  helium-4 atomic mass \(= 4.002\,603\,\mathrm{u}\);  \(1\,\mathrm{u} = 931.5\,\mathrm{MeV}\)
questions.explanation: The mass defect of helium is 0.030 377 u, giving a total binding energy of 28.30 MeV. Dividing by the four nucleons gives 7.08 MeV per nucleon — a landmark value showing helium-4 is unusually tightly bound for such a light nucleus.

questions.q: In any nuclear reaction, under what condition is energy released, and how much energy is released?
options: Energy is released when the products are heavier than the reacting nuclei, equal to the increase in mass
Energy is released when the mass of the products is less than the mass of the reacting nuclei, equal to the energy equivalent of the decrease in mass
Energy is always released in every nuclear reaction, regardless of the masses involved
Energy is released only when the total number of nucleons decreases during the reaction
questions.explanation: We can treat any nuclear reaction the same way: if the mass of the products is less than the mass of the reacting nuclei, energy is released, and the energy released is the energy equivalent to the decrease in mass.

questions.q: From memory: what does the graph of average binding energy per nucleon against mass number tell you about nuclear stability, and which is the most stable nucleus?
keyPoints: Average binding energy per nucleon measures how strongly an average nucleon is bound, and is the measure most closely related to nuclear stability.
The graph shows the most stable nuclei have a mass number of about 50 to 60; the most stable nucleus is, in fact, iron-56.
Joining light nuclei (fusion) or splitting a large nucleus in two (fission) produces nuclei with higher average binding energy per nucleon, so energy is released.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that stability is judged by binding energy per nucleon, that the peak (mass number ~50–60) is iron-56, and that both fusion and fission move toward higher binding energy per nucleon, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: Why are the separate laws of conservation of mass and conservation of energy replaced by a single law of conservation of mass-energy?
options: Because mass is destroyed in nuclear reactions and only energy survives
Because mass and energy are equivalent and can interconvert via E = mc², so neither is conserved alone — only the combined total mass-energy is conserved
Because energy is much larger than mass, so mass can be ignored entirely
Because the speed of light changes inside the nucleus, breaking both old laws
questions.explanation: Special relativity shows mass and energy are equivalent and can interconvert. In nuclear reactions mass converts into energy and vice versa, so neither mass alone nor energy alone is conserved — only the total mass-energy is conserved, fusing the two classical laws into one.

questions.q: In your own words, using the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve, explain why BOTH nuclear fission and nuclear fusion release energy.
keyPoints: The curve rises steeply from the lightest nuclei, peaks at iron-56 (the most stable nucleus), then falls slowly for heavier nuclei.
Fusion combines light nuclei from the left of the peak into a heavier nucleus higher on the curve, closer to iron, with greater binding energy per nucleon — the gain in binding energy is released.
Fission splits a heavy nucleus from the right of the peak into mid-mass fragments higher on the curve, closer to iron — again the gain in binding energy is released.
Both release energy because their products move toward the iron-56 peak, where nucleons are more tightly bound.
questions.explanation: The unified idea: reactions release energy when their products climb the curve toward the iron-56 peak. Fusion climbs from the left, fission climbs from the right, and they meet at iron — nothing releases energy moving away from iron.

questions.q: Explain the relationship between mass defect and binding energy. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The mass of a nucleus is always less than the combined mass of its separate constituent protons and neutrons; this missing mass is the mass defect. By Einstein's mass-energy equivalence, that mass was converted into energy and released when the nucleons bound together. The energy equivalent of the mass defect is the binding energy, equal to the mass defect times the speed of light squared. It is both the energy released when the nucleus forms and the energy required to separate it completely into free nucleons. A larger binding energy, and in particular a larger binding energy per nucleon, means a more tightly bound, more stable nucleus.

criteria.descriptor: Defines the mass defect as the difference between the mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus.
Links the mass defect to energy via mass-energy equivalence (binding energy = mass defect × c²).
States binding energy is both the energy released on formation and the energy needed to separate the nucleus into free nucleons.
Relates a larger binding energy (per nucleon) to a more tightly bound, more stable nucleus.

questions.explanation: The strong-answer move is to name the mass defect as the source of the energy and tie its size to c² being enormous. Never write that mass is 'destroyed' — it is converted into energy.

questions.q: Iron-56 is described as the most stable nucleus. Which statement about its binding energy is correct?
options: Iron-56 has both the highest total binding energy and the highest binding energy per nucleon of all nuclei
Iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon; heavy nuclei such as uranium have a larger total binding energy because they have far more nucleons
Iron-56 has the highest total binding energy, which is why it is the most stable
Iron-56 has the lowest binding energy per nucleon, which is why it cannot decay
questions.explanation: Stability is measured by binding energy per nucleon, and iron-56 sits at the peak of that curve. Heavy nuclei like uranium have a larger TOTAL binding energy simply because they have hundreds of nucleons to add up — but each of iron's nucleons is held more tightly, which is what 'most stable' means.
